name: Mary, mother of Jesus

seo.title: Mary, mother of Jesus: her life, her song and what churches teach
seo.description: Mary of Nazareth in plain words: her life in the Gospels, her song, her feast days, and what Catholic, Orthodox and Protestant churches believe of her.

band.lede: The mother of Jesus. She said yes to God at Nazareth, stood by the cross, and prayed with the first Christians.

who: Mary was a woman of Nazareth, pledged to marry Joseph. Luke tells how the angel Gabriel said she would bear the Son of God, and she answered, “May it happen to me according to your word.” She gave birth to Jesus in Bethlehem, stood by His cross, and prayed with the apostles after He rose.

roles.name: Exile
roles.line: In Egypt, out of Herod's reach

roles.name: Witness
roles.line: At Cana, and at the cross

lines: Four in Luke, two in John
The last: “Do whatever He tells you.”
They found Him in the temple courts
In Matthew: Tamar, Rahab, Ruth, Uriah's wife

tidbits.text: Her song, the **Magnificat**, is close in thought and words to Hannah's song in 1 Samuel 2. The Catholic Church sings it every evening, at Vespers.
Three old Latin manuscripts of Luke give her song to Elizabeth: “And Elizabeth said”. The Greek and Syriac texts all give it to Mary.
The first half of the **Hail Mary** is Luke's words: the angel's greeting, then Elizabeth's.
Before Rome defined her Assumption in 1950, more than eight million people had signed petitions asking it to, says *Britannica*.

facts.label: Born
facts.text: In a year no one recorded. The Bible does not name her parents. The *Protevangelium of James*, a book of the 100s, calls them **Joachim** and **Anna**.

facts.label: Home
facts.text: **Nazareth**, a town in Galilee. She went to Bethlehem for a census, to Egypt with Joseph, and to Jerusalem every year for the Passover.

facts.label: Family
facts.text: Pledged in marriage to **Joseph**, of the house of David. The mother of **Jesus**. **Elizabeth**, the mother of John the Baptist, was her relative. John names “her sister” at the cross.

facts.label: Name
facts.text: **Miriam** in Hebrew, the name of Moses' sister. The Greek New Testament writes it Mariam or Maria. Six women in it are called Mary.

facts.label: Also called
facts.text: **The Virgin Mary**. The **Blessed Virgin Mary**, in Catholic and Anglican calendars. The **Theotokos**, the Mother of God. **Our Lady**.

facts.label: Named in
facts.text: Matthew, Mark, Luke and Acts. John never gives her name: she is “His mother” or “Jesus' mother”. Paul writes only that God sent His Son “born of a woman”, probably the earliest mention of her, says *Britannica*.

facts.label: Died
facts.text: The Bible does not say. The last time it names her, she is at prayer in Jerusalem with the apostles. Later tradition places her death in **Jerusalem**, or at **Ephesus**.

facts.label: Buried
facts.text: No grave is known for certain. A tomb in Jerusalem is said to be hers, says *Britannica*. John of Damascus preached in the 700s that she was laid in a tomb at **Gethsemane**.

west.text: **Mary, the Holy Mother of God**, a **Catholic** solemnity.
The **Annunciation**, a **Catholic** solemnity. A Principal Feast in the **Church of England**. Also the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.
The **Visitation**, her visit to Elizabeth: a **Catholic** feast. Also the **Church of England**, the **Episcopal Church**, and Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA**.

The **Assumption**, a **Catholic** solemnity. The **Church of England** keeps **The Blessed Virgin Mary**, and the **Episcopal Church** **Saint Mary the Virgin**. Lutherans in the **Missouri Synod** and the **ELCA** keep **Mary, Mother of our Lord**.
Her **birth**, a **Catholic** feast. Also the **Church of England**.
The **Immaculate Conception**, a **Catholic** solemnity. The **Church of England** keeps **the Conception of the Blessed Virgin Mary**.

east.text: The **Coptic** Church, on 21 Tobi in its own calendar: her **Dormition**, her falling asleep.
The **Annunciation**, one of the great feasts, in the **OCA** and the **Greek** churches.
The **Dormition** of the Theotokos, in the **OCA** and the **Greek** churches.
The **Coptic** Church, on 16 Mesori: the **Assumption of her body**.
Her **Nativity**, in the **OCA** and the **Greek** churches.
The **Protection** of the Theotokos, in the **OCA**.
Her **Entry into the Temple** as a child, in the **OCA** and the **Greek** churches.
Her **Conception** by Saint Anna, in the **OCA**.
The **Synaxis** of the Theotokos, the day after Christmas, in the **OCA**.

feasts.note: Her birth on 8 September and her conception on 8 or 9 December are nine months apart. Both halves of the Church keep her conception, but they differ on what it means: see What the churches believe about her, below. The Coptic Church keeps her death in January and the taking up of her body in August. Churches on the old calendar keep each date 13 days later, so their Dormition falls on 28 August.

quotes.q: Greetings, you who are highly favored! The Lord is with you.
Blessed are you among women, and blessed is the fruit of your womb! And why am I so honored, that the mother of my Lord should come to me?
quotes.who: Elizabeth, filled with the Holy Spirit, when Mary came to her door

quotes.q: Behold, this Child is appointed to cause the rise and fall of many in Israel, and to be a sign that will be spoken against, so that the thoughts of many hearts will be revealed—and a sword will pierce your soul as well.
quotes.who: Simeon, holding the baby Jesus in the temple, to His mother

quotes.q: Now the virginity of Mary was hidden from the prince of this world, as was also her offspring, and the death of the Lord; three mysteries of renown, which were wrought in silence by God.
quotes.who: Ignatius of Antioch, writing to the Christians of Ephesus, about 110

cite.text: Ignatius, Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 19

quotes.q: And thus also it was that the knot of Eve's disobedience was loosed by the obedience of Mary. For what the virgin Eve had bound fast through unbelief, this did the virgin Mary set free through faith.
When the apostles fled, she stood at the Cross, and with pious eyes beheld her Son's wounds, for she did not look for the death of her Offspring, but the salvation of the world.
quotes.who: Ambrose, bishop of Milan, in a letter to the church at Vercelli

quotes.q: We see how Mary makes herself nothing, and praises God alone.

moments.title: The angel's greeting
moments.text: God sent the angel Gabriel to a virgin in Nazareth, pledged in marriage to a man named Joseph. Mary was greatly troubled at his greeting. “Do not be afraid, Mary, for you have found favor with God.” She would bear a Son, and call Him Jesus. “How can this be,” Mary asked the angel, “since I am a virgin?” The Holy Spirit would come upon her, he said. Her relative Elizabeth, called barren, was already six months pregnant. “For no word from God will ever fail.” Mary answered, “I am the Lord's servant. May it happen to me according to your word.”

moments.title: The visit to Elizabeth
moments.text: Mary got ready and hurried to the home of Zechariah and Elizabeth. When Elizabeth heard her greeting, the baby leaped in her womb, and she was filled with the Holy Spirit. She called Mary blessed among women, “the mother of my Lord”. Mary answered with a song of praise, the Magnificat: see Her words, below. She stayed about three months, then went home.

moments.title: Joseph's dream
moments.text: Mary was pledged in marriage to Joseph, but before they came together, “she was found to be with child through the Holy Spirit.” Joseph was a righteous man. He did not want to disgrace her publicly, so he resolved to divorce her quietly. Then an angel of the Lord spoke to him in a dream: “Joseph, son of David, do not be afraid to embrace Mary as your wife, for the One conceived in her is from the Holy Spirit.” When he woke, he took her home as his wife.

moments.title: No room in the inn
moments.text: An order from Caesar Augustus sent Joseph to Bethlehem, the city of David, to register with Mary. While they were there, she gave birth to her firstborn, a Son. She wrapped Him in swaddling cloths and laid Him in a manger, “because there was no room for them in the inn.” Shepherds came from the fields, sent by an angel, and told what they had heard. All who heard them were amazed. “But Mary treasured up all these things and pondered them in her heart.”

moments.title: The sword foretold
moments.text: Mary and Joseph brought the Child to Jerusalem to present Him to the Lord. They offered the sacrifice the Law of the Lord specified: “A pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons.” An old man named Simeon, who had been waiting for the Lord's Christ, took Jesus in his arms and blessed God. Then he turned to Mary. Her Son would be a sign spoken against, he said, and a sword would pierce her own soul. An aged prophetess, Anna, gave thanks and spoke about the Child to all who were waiting.

moments.title: The flight into Egypt
moments.text: Magi from the east came to the house, and “saw the Child with His mother Mary”. They fell down and worshiped Him, and gave Him gold, frankincense and myrrh. Then an angel warned Joseph in a dream: “Take the Child and His mother and flee to Egypt.” They left by night, and stayed until Herod died. Then they came back, and settled in Nazareth.

moments.when: The Passover, when He was twelve
moments.title: Lost and found in the temple
moments.text: Every year the family went to Jerusalem for the Passover. When Jesus was twelve, He stayed behind, and His parents did not know. After three days they found Him in the temple courts, sitting among the teachers. “Child, why have You done this to us?” His mother asked. “Your father and I have been anxiously searching for You.” He answered, “Did you not know that I had to be in My Father's house?” They did not understand. He went home with them and was obedient to them. “But His mother treasured up all these things in her heart.”

moments.title: The wine runs out
moments.text: Mary was at a wedding at Cana, and Jesus and His disciples were invited too. When the wine ran out, she said to Him, “They have no more wine.” “Woman, what is that to you and to Me?” Jesus replied. “My hour has not yet come.” His mother said to the servants, “Do whatever He tells you.” Jesus had them fill six stone jars with water, and the water became wine. John calls it “the first of His signs”.

moments.title: “Who is My mother?”
moments.text: Once His mother and brothers came to see Him, but could not reach Him for the crowd. Jesus pointed to His disciples. “Here are My mother and My brothers. For whoever does the will of My Father in heaven is My brother and sister and mother.” Another day a woman in the crowd called out, “Blessed is the womb that bore You.” He replied, “Blessed rather are those who hear the word of God and obey it.” Augustine read both sayings as praise of Mary herself: “Mary is more blessed in receiving the faith of Christ, than in conceiving the flesh of Christ.”

cite.text: Matthew 12:46-50; Luke 11:27-28; Augustine, On Holy Virginity, chapter 3

moments.title: At the cross
moments.text: Near the cross of Jesus stood His mother and her sister, with Mary the wife of Clopas and Mary Magdalene. Jesus saw His mother, and the disciple whom He loved standing nearby. He said to His mother, “Woman, here is your son.” Then He said to the disciple, “Here is your mother.” “So from that hour, this disciple took her into his home.”

moments.title: At prayer with the apostles
moments.text: After Jesus was taken up, the eleven apostles went back to the upper room where they were staying. “With one accord they all continued in prayer, along with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus, and with His brothers.” It is the last time the Bible names her.

words.note: Mary wrote nothing. The Gospels give her words six times: her questions and answers are in her life, above. Her longest words are a song, spoken at Elizabeth's house, known by its first word in Latin, the Magnificat. Outside the quiz's own section, every Bible line on this page is from the Berean Standard Bible.

feature.q: My soul magnifies the Lord, and my spirit rejoices in God my Savior!
feature.ctx: Elizabeth had just called her blessed. Mary answered with a song of praise to God.

quotes.q: For He has looked with favor on the humble state of His servant. From now on all generations will call me blessed.
For the Mighty One has done great things for me. Holy is His name. His mercy extends to those who fear Him, from generation to generation.
He has brought down rulers from their thrones, but has exalted the humble. He has filled the hungry with good things, but has sent the rich away empty.
He has helped His servant Israel, remembering to be merciful, as He promised to our fathers, to Abraham and his descendants forever.

myths.claim: The Immaculate Conception means Jesus was conceived without a human father.
myths.truth: That is the virgin birth, told in Matthew and Luke. The Immaculate Conception is a different teaching, about Mary's own conception. The Catholic Church defined it in 1854: from the first instant of her conception, she was kept free of original sin. See What the churches believe about her, below.

cite.text: Matthew 1:18; Luke 1:34-35; Ineffabilis Deus (1854), in Philip Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom

myths.claim: Mary rode a donkey to Bethlehem.
myths.truth: Luke does not say how they travelled. Joseph went “to register with Mary, who was pledged to him in marriage and was expecting a child.” The donkey comes from the *Protevangelium of James*, a book of the 100s that never became part of the Bible. There Joseph “saddled the ass, and set her upon it; and his son led it”.

cite.text: Luke 2:4-5; Protevangelium of James, chapter 17, Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 8

myths.truth: No innkeeper appears in the story. Luke says only that she laid her Son in a manger, “because there was no room for them in the inn.”

myths.claim: Mary was fourteen when the angel came.
myths.truth: The Bible gives no age. The *Protevangelium of James* says “she was sixteen years old when these mysteries happened”. Its manuscripts differ: one says fourteen, two say fifteen, and one says seventeen.

cite.text: Protevangelium of James, chapter 12, with the notes in the Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 8

myths.truth: Both churches say worship belongs to God alone. In 787 the Second Council of Nicaea, which both accept, approved images of Christ, of “our spotless Lady, the Mother of God”, and of the saints. They were to be given honour, “not indeed that true worship of faith (latreian) which pertains alone to the divine nature”. Protestant confessions object to calling on the saints in prayer: see Asking her prayers, below.

cite.text: Second Council of Nicaea, the definition, Nicene and Post-Nicene Fathers, second series, volume 14

myths.claim: Mary spent her last years in a house near Ephesus.
myths.truth: The Bible does not say where she lived after the cross. The house shown near Ephesus was found by searchers following the visions of Catherine Emmerich, a nun. The *Catholic Encyclopedia* weighed the old claims for Ephesus and for Jerusalem. It judged that “the evidence for her permanent home in Jerusalem is much stronger”.

extras.title: What the churches believe about her
extras.lede: All three honour Mary, in different ways. The early councils gave her one great title. On three other questions the churches differ, and here each speaks for itself. How they see the end of her life is below.

items.title: Mother of God
items.text: The early Church called her the *Theotokos*, Greek for “giving birth to God”. The title is about who her Son is. In 431 the Council of Ephesus condemned Nestorius, bishop of Constantinople, who would call her only “mother of Christ”. The council heard this letter from Cyril of Alexandria. Catholics pray, “Holy Mary, Mother of God”. The Orthodox catechism calls it a great title. The Lutheran *Formula of Concord* (1577) says “she is both rightly called and in very deed is the Mother of God.”
items.quote: They ventured to call the holy Virgin, the Mother of God, not as if the nature of the Word or His divinity had its beginning from the holy Virgin, but because of her was born that holy body with a rational soul, to which the Word being personally united is said to be born according to the flesh.

cite.text: Cyril of Alexandria, Second Letter to Nestorius, at the Council of Ephesus; the Formula of Concord, Epitome, article 8; Britannica; Merriam-Webster

items.title: Conceived without sin?
items.text: **The Catholic Church** teaches that God kept Mary free of original sin from the first instant of her conception. Pope Pius IX defined it in 1854. It was a gift given “in view of the merits of Christ Jesus the Saviour of mankind”. In Catholic teaching, Christ saved her too, by keeping her from it. **The Orthodox** honour her as most pure. Their catechism speaks of Christ and “His immaculate Mother”. But they do not accept the 1854 teaching. The Patriarch of Constantinople wrote in 1895 that it was new, unknown to the ancient Church. **Protestant churches** do not hold it either. The Protestant historian Philip Schaff pointed to Luke 1:47, where she calls God her Savior. So she “includes herself in the number of the redeemed”, he wrote.

cite.text: Ineffabilis Deus (1854) and the Longer Catechism, question 520, in Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom, volume 2; the Patriarchal Encyclical of 1895, chapter 13; Schaff, volume 1

items.title: Ever a virgin? The brothers of Jesus
items.text: The three traditions agree that she was a virgin when she conceived Jesus. After His birth, they differ. **The Catholic Church** holds that she stayed a virgin all her life. Jerome wrote in 383, “We believe that God was born of the Virgin, because we read it. That Mary was married after she brought forth, we do not believe, because we do not read it.” Catholics read the brothers as “His cousins or the more or less near relatives”. **The Orthodox** call her ever-virgin, a virgin “before the birth, during the birth, and after the birth”. The OCA calls James a son of Joseph by an earlier wife. **Protestants** differ. The *Second Helvetic Confession* (1566) calls her “Mary, who was always a virgin”. Many read the brothers, with the historian Philip Schaff, as “younger children of Joseph and Mary”.
items.quote: Isn't this the carpenter, the son of Mary and the brother of James, Joses, Judas, and Simon? Aren't His sisters here with us as well?

cite.text: Mark 6:3; Jerome, Against Helvidius, chapter 21; Catholic Encyclopedia; the Longer Catechism, question 186; the OCA, 23 October; the Second Helvetic Confession, chapter 11; Schaff, History of the Christian Church, volume 1

items.title: Asking her prayers
items.text: **The Catholic Church** teaches that the saints pray for us, and “that it is good and useful suppliantly to invoke them”, as the Council of Trent put it. The Hail Mary ends, “Holy Mary, Mother of God, pray for us sinners now and at the hour of our death.” **The Orthodox** ask her prayers too. Their catechism says the Church “calls upon Christ our true God, by the prayers of His most pure Mother and all His saints.” **Protestant confessions** do not call on her. The Lutheran *Augsburg Confession* (1530) says “the memory of saints may be set before us, that we may follow their faith and good works”. But “the Scripture teacheth not to invocate saints, or to ask help of saints, because it propoundeth unto us one Christ the Mediator”.

cite.text: Council of Trent, session 25; Catholic Encyclopedia, “Hail Mary”; the Longer Catechism, question 264; the Augsburg Confession, article 21, in Schaff, The Creeds of Christendom

circle.name: Joseph
circle.text: Her husband, of the house of David. Four times a dream guided him: to marry her, to flee to Egypt, to come back, and to settle in Galilee. Each time he obeyed.

circle.name: Elizabeth
circle.text: Her relative, the wife of the priest Zechariah. She conceived in her old age, and was the first to call Mary “the mother of my Lord”.

circle.name: John the Baptist
circle.text: Elizabeth's son. When Mary's greeting reached his mother's ears, the baby leaped for joy in her womb.

circle.name: Simeon
circle.text: A righteous old man in Jerusalem, promised he would see the Christ before he died. He took the Child in his arms, and warned Mary of the sword.

circle.name: Anna
circle.text: A prophetess of the tribe of Asher, who never left the temple. She gave thanks for the Child and spoke of Him to all who waited.

circle.name: The disciple whom Jesus loved
circle.text: From the cross Jesus gave her to him as his mother, and he took her into his home. Tradition names him as John the apostle.

cite.text: John 19:26-27; Catholic Encyclopedia, “The Blessed Virgin Mary”

circle.name: Mary Magdalene
circle.text: She stood near the cross with Jesus' mother. On the first day of the week, she went to the tomb.

circle.name: Mary the wife of Clopas
circle.text: She too stood by the cross. John also names “her sister” there: many take the two to be the same woman.

cite.text: John 19:25; Strong's Greek 3137, with Thayer's lexicon

circle.name: The brothers of Jesus
circle.text: James, Joses, Judas and Simon, with sisters not named. At first “even His own brothers did not believe in Him.” After He rose, they prayed with Mary in the upper room. Who they were is argued: see above.

death.title: The end of her life
death.big: The Bible does not say how or when her life ended. It last names her at prayer with the apostles, before Pentecost.
paras: At the cross Jesus gave her to the disciple He loved, and “from that hour, this disciple took her into his home.” Where they lived is not told.

Later Christians told of her death, and of her body taken up to heaven. John of Damascus, preaching in the 700s, said she was laid in a tomb at Gethsemane: “Then it was assumed after three days to the heavenly mansions.” The churches hold this in different ways.

**The Catholic Church.** In 1950 Pope Pius XII defined that Mary was taken up to heaven, body and soul. His Latin reads {la|Immaculatam Deiparam semper Virginem Mariam, expleto terrestris vitae cursu, fuisse corpore et anima ad caelestem gloriam assumptam}. In our translation: “the Immaculate Mother of God, the ever-Virgin Mary, having completed the course of her earthly life, was taken up body and soul into heavenly glory.” The feast is the Assumption, on 15 August.

**The Orthodox Church** keeps the same day as the Dormition, her falling asleep. John of Damascus preached, “Thy pure and spotless body was not left in the earth.” The OCA tells the old account. The apostles buried her at Gethsemane. Thomas came late, and on the third day they opened the tomb for him. They found only her grave wrappings.

**Protestant confessions** teach neither. They hold to Scripture alone for doctrine, as the Church of England's *Thirty-nine Articles* put it: “whatsoever is not read therein, nor may be proved thereby, is not to be required of any man, that it should be believed as an article of the Faith.” The Church of England, the Episcopal Church and many Lutherans still keep 15 August, as a feast of Mary herself.

later.title: Thomas and her girdle
later.text: A later writing, *The Passing of Mary*, tells more, in a Latin form known from manuscripts of the 1200s. Thomas, carried from India, saw her body “going up into heaven”. She threw him her girdle. When the apostles opened the tomb, “they did not find the body”. The book was never part of the Bible.

cite.text: The Passing of Mary, First Latin Form, Ante-Nicene Fathers, volume 8

saint.big: Yes. Every church that keeps saints' days honours her, most of them on 15 August.

churches.note: A Festival in the Church of England

paras: The Orthodox catechism says the Church “honors her far above the cherubim and seraphim”.

Churches that keep no saints' days honour her too. In 1655 the Waldensian churches of Piedmont were accused of despising her. They answered that they “hold above all the holy Virgin Mary to be ‘blessed amongst women.’”
She had said so herself, in her song: “From now on all generations will call me blessed.”

kin.name: Hannah
kin.text: She prayed for a son and gave him to God. Her song, “My heart rejoices in the LORD”, is the one Mary's echoes.

kin.name: Ruth
kin.text: A foreigner who became David's great-grandmother. Matthew names her in the family tree of Jesus, with Mary last.

kin.name: Judith
kin.text: After she saved her people, Ozias blessed her “above all the women upon the earth”. Elizabeth blessed Mary “among women”.
